drills.los_text: describe the factors affecting fixed-income portfolio returns due to a change in benchmark yields

questions.stem: The expected return on a fixed-income portfolio is most likely decomposed into:

options.A: coupon income and price change only.
options.B: yield-to-maturity alone.
options.C: coupon income, rolldown return, and expected price changes from yield, spread and currency views.

rationales.A: Coupon income plus an undifferentiated price change is too coarse. It folds rolldown return together with the three distinct expected price change terms and so gives the manager nothing to act on: the decomposition exists to separate the part of return earned simply by holding the bond as it ages down the curve from the parts that depend on the investor's views of benchmark yields, yield spreads and currency values.
rationales.B: Yield-to-maturity is a single summary yield measure, not a decomposition of expected return. It assumes the bond is held to maturity with coupons reinvested at that same yield, and it says nothing about rolldown or about the price effects of the manager's yield, spread and currency views over a holding period shorter than the bond's life.
rationales.C: Expected return decomposes into five components: E(R) is approximately equal to coupon income, plus or minus rolldown return, plus or minus the expected price change due to the investor's view of benchmark yields, plus or minus the expected price change due to the investor's view of yield spreads, plus or minus the expected price change due to the investor's view of currency value changes. Coupon income and rolldown return together make up the return earned if the yield curve does not move, while the three expected price change terms capture the active views. Yield curve strategies actively manage the first three components; currency is added separately, and credit or spread strategies are treated with the fourth.

questions.stem: A yield curve is best described as:

options.A: a fixed curve identical for every investor and every use.
options.B: the curve of on-the-run bonds only.
options.C: a stylized representation of yields-to-maturity available at various maturities for an issuer.

rationales.A: There is no single unambiguous curve. Yield curve models rest on assumptions that vary by investor and by intended use, and the choice of issuer or issuer group, of which bonds to include and of how to fill maturity gaps all change the resulting curve, so two careful analysts can draw different curves from the same market.
rationales.B: Restricting the curve to on-the-run issues is one construction choice among several, not the definition. Off-the-run bonds can be included, and doing so changes the curve, because off-the-run issues are less liquid and trade at higher yields-to-maturity, which pulls the fitted curve higher.
rationales.C: A yield curve is a stylized representation of the yields-to-maturity available at various maturities for a specific issuer or group of issuers. Because it is a representation rather than a direct observation, its construction raises issues such as asynchronous observations of individual bond prices, maturity gaps that require interpolation or smoothing, apparent outliers, the choice between on-the-run and off-the-run bonds, and differences in accounting, regulatory and tax treatment across issues and investors. Yield curve models make assumptions on each of these points that vary by investor or intended use, so different models produce different curves.

questions.stem: Compared with on-the-run bonds, off-the-run bonds are most likely:

options.A: more liquid, with lower yields-to-maturity.
options.B: less liquid, with higher yields-to-maturity.

rationales.A: This reverses the liquidity relationship. The on-the-run issue is the most recently auctioned and most actively traded security at its maturity; the off-the-run issues it displaced trade less, so they command a liquidity concession, not a liquidity premium in price.
rationales.B: Off-the-run bonds are typically less liquid than on-the-run bonds and hence have a lower price, which is to say a higher yield-to-maturity. Including off-the-run bonds therefore tends to pull the fitted yield curve higher than a curve built from on-the-run issues alone. This is one of the reasons different yield curve constructions produce different curves from the same market, and it is why the construction choice has to be stated before curve levels or spreads are compared.
rationales.C: Liquidity differs meaningfully between the two, and price differs with it. The newly issued on-the-run bond concentrates trading activity, while older off-the-run issues of similar maturity trade at lower prices and higher yields, so treating them as interchangeable misstates the curve.

questions.stem: A constant maturity yield is most likely estimated by:

options.A: interpolating yields-to-maturity on actively traded bonds with nearby maturities.
options.B: using zero-coupon rates only.
options.C: using the current on-the-run bond's yield.

rationales.A: A constant maturity yield estimates what a hypothetical yield-to-maturity would be if a bond were available with exactly the target maturity, for example exactly five years. No such bond generally exists, because the on-the-run five-year note was issued before today and so has a remaining maturity of less than five years. Estimating a constant maturity five-year yield therefore requires interpolating the yields-to-maturity on actively traded bonds with maturities near five years. Some derivatives reference the daily constant maturity yield, which is why the series is published even though it corresponds to no traded security.
rationales.B: Zero-coupon rates are not what the constant maturity series is built from. It is derived from the yields-to-maturity of actively traded coupon bonds near the target maturity; a zero-coupon curve answers a different question and would itself require bootstrapping or fitting from those same traded issues.
rationales.C: The current on-the-run bond has a remaining maturity of less than the target, since it was issued at some point before today. Taking its yield as the constant maturity yield therefore prices the wrong point on the curve, which is the gap interpolation is meant to close.

questions.stem: Principal components analysis of historical US Treasury yield curve changes most likely identifies the primary yield curve risk factors as:

options.A: central bank policy risk alone.
options.B: level, slope, and curvature.
options.C: three forms of issuer-specific credit risk.

rationales.A: The decomposition yields three factors, not one. Level (a parallel shift) accounts for roughly 82% of US Treasury yield curve changes, slope (a flattening or steepening twist) roughly 12%, and curvature or shape (butterfly movement) roughly 4%. Central bank policy influences the short end of the curve, but it is not itself one of the statistically derived factors.
rationales.B: Primary yield curve risk factors are categorized by three types: (1) change in level (a parallel shift), (2) change in slope (a flattening or steepening twist), and (3) change in shape or curvature (butterfly movement). Principal components analysis used to decompose yield curve changes shows that level, slope, and curvature movements over time accounted for approximately 82%, 12%, and 4%, respectively, of US Treasury yield curve changes. The consistency of these results over time and across global markets underscores their importance in active yield curve strategies.
rationales.C: Issuer-specific credit risk is a separate factor family from yield curve risk: a change in a credit spread is not a movement in the underlying government curve. The three factors extracted by principal components analysis are level, slope, and curvature, which together explain roughly 98% of curve movement.

questions.stem: Yield curve slope is most likely measured as:

options.A: the standard deviation of yields across maturities.
options.B: the average yield across all maturities.
options.C: the yield difference between a long-maturity and a shorter-maturity bond.

rationales.A: Standard deviation measures the dispersion of yields across the maturity spectrum, which says nothing about direction. Slope is a directional difference: the long-maturity yield-to-maturity less the shorter-maturity yield-to-maturity. A curve could show wide yield dispersion and still be flat in the long-minus-short sense.
rationales.B: An average yield across maturities describes the level of the curve, the factor that accounts for roughly 82% of curve changes, not its slope. Slope is the difference between the yields-to-maturity at the long and short ends.
rationales.C: Yield curve slope is the difference in basis points between the yield-to-maturity on a long-maturity bond and the yield-to-maturity on a shorter-maturity bond. For instance, as of July 2020 the slope measured by the 2s30s spread — the 30-year Treasury bond at 1.43% less the 2-year Treasury note at 0.16% — was 127 bps. As the spread widens the curve steepens; as it narrows the curve flattens; if the spread turns negative, as it did just before the 2008 global financial crisis, the yield curve is inverted.

questions.stem: The butterfly spread used to measure yield curve curvature is most likely calculated as:

options.A: twice the medium-term yield less the short-term and long-term yields.
options.B: the short-term and long-term yields less twice the medium-term yield.
options.C: the long-term yield less the short-term yield.

rationales.A: Butterfly spread = −(Short-term yield) + (2 × Medium-term yield) − Long-term yield. The butterfly spread takes on larger positive values when the yield curve has more curvature. A positive butterfly spread indicates a humped or concave shape at the midpoint of the curve; a negative butterfly spread indicates a saucer or convex shape. The spread changes when intermediate-term yield changes are of a different magnitude than those on the wings (the short and long ends), and it is commonly computed from the 2-year, 10-year, and 30-year tenors.
rationales.B: The signs are reversed. The medium-term yield carries the positive weight of 2 and both wings are subtracted: −(Short-term yield) + (2 × Medium-term yield) − Long-term yield. As specified here, the measure returns the negative of the butterfly spread, so it would label a humped (concave) curve a saucer and a saucer a hump.
rationales.C: The long yield less the short yield is the slope of the curve, a two-point measure. Curvature requires three points, with the medium-term yield weighted by 2 against the short and long wings, which is what the butterfly spread does.

questions.stem: The percentage change in a bond's full price for a given change in yield is most likely estimated by:

options.A: modified duration times the yield change.
options.B: minus modified duration times the yield change, plus a convexity adjustment.

rationales.A: This omits the convexity term and carries the wrong sign on the duration term. The duration effect is negative: a rise in yield lowers price. Without the second-order convexity adjustment, the estimate also overstates the loss when yields rise and understates the gain when yields fall.
rationales.B: %ΔPV_Full ≈ −(ModDur × ΔYield) + [½ × Convexity × (ΔYield)²]. Duration is a first-order (linear) effect and convexity is a second-order (curvature) correction. For a portfolio, market-value-weighted averages of modified duration and convexity are substituted into the same relationship. Duration is the first-order effect and typically dominates portfolio performance, so duration management (accounting for level changes) is usually more important than convexity management. Convexity management is more closely associated with yield curve slope and shape changes.
rationales.C: This omits the duration term, which is the first-order effect and typically dominates the price change. Convexity on its own is only the second-order correction, scaled by one-half and by the square of the yield change, so it is small for small yield moves and positive for either direction of yield change.

questions.stem: Portfolio A is a bullet holding only the 5-year Treasury note, with modified duration of 4.88 and convexity of 26.5. Portfolio B is a barbell of 2-year and 10-year Treasuries with the same 4.88 modified duration but convexity of 40.229. If all yields fall by 50 bps, Portfolio B most likely:

options.A: Gains less than Portfolio A.
options.B: Loses value while Portfolio A gains.

rationales.A: Portfolio B carries the higher convexity (40.229 versus 26.5) at the same 4.88 modified duration, so the second-order term adds more to its return when yields fall. Its gain exceeds the bullet's rather than falling short of it.
rationales.B: Both portfolios gain when yields fall. Each has a modified duration of about 4.88, so the first-order duration effect alone is a price increase of roughly 2.44% for a 50 bp decline, and the convexity term is positive, adding to that gain for both.
rationales.C: For a 50 bp decline in yields, Portfolio A returns +2.473% ($1,236,563) and Portfolio B returns +2.490% ($1,245,170) on a $50 million portfolio, so Portfolio B gains $8,607 more, due entirely to its higher convexity (40.229 versus 26.5) at the same modified duration. The asymmetry favors the barbell in both directions: on a 50 bp rise in yields, Portfolio A returns −2.407% ($1,203,438) against Portfolio B's −2.390% ($1,194,883), a loss $8,555 smaller for Portfolio B.

questions.stem: All else equal, higher positive convexity in a bond is most likely valuable because:

options.A: it deepens the price loss when yields rise.
options.B: it raises the price gain and limits the price loss relative to the duration estimate.
options.C: it offers no net benefit, since its effects offset across yield moves.

rationales.A: Convexity cushions losses rather than deepening them. Of two bonds with the same duration, the one with higher positive convexity falls less in price when yields rise, because the second-order term, ½ × Convexity × (ΔYield)², is positive for either direction of yield change.
rationales.B: All else equal, positive convexity is a valuable feature in bonds. If a bond has higher positive convexity than an otherwise identical bond, then the bond price increases more if interest rates decrease, and decreases less if interest rates increase, than the duration estimate would suggest. This price behavior is valuable to investors; therefore a bond with higher convexity might be expected to have a lower yield-to-maturity than a similar-duration bond with less convexity. Convexity itself is affected by cash flow dispersion: higher dispersion produces higher convexity.
rationales.C: The two effects reinforce one another rather than cancelling. The convexity term is positive whether the yield change is positive or negative, so the holder gains more when rates fall and loses less when rates rise. That asymmetry is what investors pay for, which is why a higher-convexity bond can be expected to trade at a lower yield-to-maturity than a similar-duration bond with less convexity.

questions.stem: For two portfolios of equal duration, the relationship between cash flow dispersion and convexity is most likely that:

options.A: dispersion does not affect convexity.
options.B: higher dispersion lowers convexity, leaving barbells less convex than bullets.
options.C: higher dispersion raises convexity, leaving barbells more convex than bullets.

rationales.A: Cash flow dispersion is what creates convexity, so the two are not independent. Convexity depends on the variance of the times to receipt of cash flow, and spreading cash flows away from the duration point raises it directly.
rationales.B: The relationship runs the other way: dispersion raises convexity, and a barbell has more convexity than a bullet of the same duration. A barbell's cash flows sit at the short and long wings, giving a high variance of times to receipt, while a bullet's are concentrated around its single maturity.
rationales.C: Convexity is affected by the dispersion of cash flows — the variance of the times to receipt of cash flow. Higher cash flow dispersion leads to an increase in convexity. This is in contrast to Macaulay duration, which measures the weighted average of the times to cash flow receipt. All else equal, bonds with longer durations also have higher convexity. Dispersion is why a barbell of 2-year and 10-year Treasuries shows convexity of 40.229 against 26.5 for a 5-year bullet with the same 4.88 modified duration.

drills.los_text: formulate a portfolio positioning strategy given forward interest rates and an interest rate view that coincides with the market view

questions.stem: A manager whose yield curve forecast matches the current curve most likely seeks excess return versus the benchmark index by:

options.A: adding duration or leverage.
options.B: selling all bond holdings.

rationales.A: The two basic ways to actively position a bond portfolio versus a benchmark index to generate excess return from a static or stable yield curve are to increase risk by adding either duration or leverage to the portfolio. If the yield curve is upward-sloping, longer duration exposure results in a higher yield-to-maturity over time. The repo carry trade — the difference between the higher-yielding instrument purchased and the lower-yielding financing instrument — generates excess return from the leverage route.
rationales.B: Selling all bond holdings exits fixed-income exposure entirely, forgoing the coupon income and rolldown that a static upward-sloping curve is expected to deliver, and it is not an active position taken versus the benchmark.
rationales.C: Taking duration to zero abandons the bond return the static curve is expected to deliver. With an upward-sloping curve, the manager acting on a static view wants more duration exposure, not none.

questions.stem: A static yield curve strategy implemented with cash bonds is least likely to involve:

options.A: writing callable bonds for premium income.
options.B: holding bonds to maturity without active trading.

rationales.A: Writing callable bonds to earn premium income is a volatility strategy, taken when the manager expects realized volatility to fall short of implied volatility; it is not a static yield curve strategy. The three cash-based static yield curve strategies are: (1) buy-and-hold, (2) rolling down the yield curve, and (3) the repo carry trade, in which the bond purchase is financed in the repo market and repo carry is earned when the coupon plus rolldown exceeds the financing cost.
rationales.B: Buy-and-hold is one of the three cash-based static strategies: the portfolio is held constant without active trading, and given a static curve view the manager may add duration beyond the benchmark target to capture the higher yield available further out an upward-sloping curve.
rationales.C: Rolling down the yield curve is one of the three cash-based static strategies: the portfolio is held constant and earns the price change as the bonds' maturities shorten, so the extra return comes from the passage of time and the ability to sell at a higher price.

questions.stem: Rolling down the yield curve is most likely:

options.A: continuously shifting the portfolio into shorter maturities as time passes.
options.B: buying bonds maturing beyond the horizon and selling them later at a higher price.
options.C: selling bonds immediately at the purchase date to capture the entry spread.

rationales.A: No shifting of the portfolio is required. The bond's own aging carries it down an upward-sloping curve, lowering its yield-to-maturity and lifting its price; buying shorter maturities as time passes would instead give up that rolldown.
rationales.B: Rolling down the yield curve incorporates coupon income, adjusted over time for any price difference from par, but also additional return from the passage of time and the investor's ability to sell the shorter-maturity bond in the future at a higher price, reflecting the lower yield-to-maturity along the upward-sloping curve as the bond has aged. If the yield curve is upward-sloping, buying bonds with maturity beyond the investment horizon offers a total return — higher coupon plus price appreciation — greater than the purchase of a bond with maturity matching the investment horizon, provided the curve remains static.
rationales.C: Selling at the purchase date captures nothing: the strategy holds the bond precisely so that the price appreciation from riding down the upward-sloping curve accrues to the portfolio.

questions.stem: The repo carry trade is most likely:

options.A: Buying a short-term security and financing it at a long-term rate.
options.B: Borrowing at long-term rates and lending at short-term rates.
options.C: Buying a long-term security and financing it at a short-term repo rate.

rationales.A: That inverts the carry. Financing at a higher long-term rate against a lower short-term yield produces negative carry; the repo carry trade buys the long-term security and finances it at the lower short-term repo rate.
rationales.B: That reverses the direction of the trade. The repo carry trade funds long-term bond positions at lower short-term repo rates, not the other way round.
rationales.C: The repo carry trade buys a long-term security and finances it at a short-term rate below the long-term YTM, earning a positive 'repo carry'. At the end of the trade the bond is sold and the repo is unwound. The trade uses the repo market for leverage: it is a cash-based strategy, but with leverage risk added.

questions.stem: Derivatives-based static yield curve strategies that synthetically increase duration most likely include:

options.A: Short-only positions that reduce duration.
options.B: Long futures positions and receive-fixed swaps.
options.C: Cash bond purchases with no derivatives.

rationales.A: Both of the positions at issue add duration synthetically: a long futures position and a receive-fixed swap are duration-extending, not duration-reducing, so short-only positions cannot be the strategies used to increase duration synthetically.
rationales.B: The derivatives-based static strategies that synthetically increase duration are (1) a long futures position, purchasing a contract for future bond delivery, with targeted return = (ΔPrice / ΔBond yield) − Margin cost; and (2) a receive-fixed swap, the fixed-rate receiver on an interest rate swap, with targeted return = (Swap rate − MRR) + (ΔSwap MTM / ΔSwap yield). The long futures position relies on price appreciation, while the receive-fixed swap generates 'swap carry' by receiving the fixed swap rate and paying MRR, much as the cash-based repo carry trade earns repo carry.
rationales.C: These are derivatives strategies, not cash strategies. The instruments involved are long futures positions and receive-fixed swaps, so cash bond purchases alone do not describe them.

questions.stem: Derivatives have a high degree of implicit leverage most likely because:

options.A: Clearinghouses require one-for-one collateralization.
options.B: The initial cash outlay is limited to margin or collateral.
options.C: Full cash payment equal to notional value is required upfront.

rationales.A: Margin-based exposure is itself the implicit leverage. Posted collateral is a fraction of notional rather than one-for-one, which is precisely why a derivative position controls far more exposure than the cash committed to it.
rationales.B: Since the initial cash outlay for a derivative is limited to initial margin or collateral, as opposed to the full price for a cash bond purchase, derivatives have a high degree of implicit leverage. A small move in price or yield can have a very large effect on a derivative's mark-to-market value relative to the margin posted. This outsized price effect makes derivatives effective instruments for fixed-income portfolio management.
rationales.C: Full upfront payment is the opposite of the leverage mechanism. Only initial margin or collateral is posted, not the notional amount, and that gap between exposure and cash committed is the source of the leverage.

questions.stem: The mandating of derivatives central counterparty (CCP) clearing after the 2008 global financial crisis most likely means that:

options.A: OTC derivatives are prohibited.
options.B: OTC derivatives face no margin requirements.
options.C: OTC derivatives face similar cash flow implications.

rationales.A: OTC derivatives continue to exist under CCP clearing. The mandate changed how they are cleared and margined, not whether they may be used.
rationales.B: CCP clearing extended margining to the OTC market rather than exempting it, so OTC positions do carry margin and collateral requirements.
rationales.C: Derivatives central counterparty (CCP) clearing, mandated by regulatory authorities following the 2008 global financial crisis to mitigate counterparty risk, has given rise to cash flow implications for OTC derivatives similar to those long faced by exchange-traded derivatives. Active managers using both exchange-traded and OTC derivatives must therefore maintain sufficient cash or eligible collateral to fulfill margin or collateral requirements. They must also factor any resulting foregone portfolio return into their overall performance.

questions.stem: The basis point value (BPV) of a government bond futures contract is most likely:

options.A: The cheapest-to-deliver bond's BPV divided by its conversion factor.
options.B: Notional value divided by margin.
options.C: The cheapest-to-deliver bond's BPV multiplied by its conversion factor.

rationales.A: Futures BPV ≈ BPV_CTD / CF_CTD, where CF_CTD is the conversion factor for the cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) security. The 'duration' of the bond futures contract is assumed to match that of the CTD security, and most government bond futures are traded and settled using the least-costly, or CTD, bond. The Ultra 10-Year US Treasury Note futures contract, for example, specifies delivery of an original 10-year issue Treasury with 9–9.5 years to maturity, an assumed 6% YTM and a contract size of $100,000. For government bond futures with a fixed underlying basket, such as Australian Treasury bond futures, futures BPV equals the BPV of the underlying basket.
rationales.B: Notional value divided by margin measures futures leverage, not the sensitivity of the contract's value to a one basis point change in yield.
rationales.C: This inverts the correct relation. The CTD bond's BPV is divided by its conversion factor, not multiplied by it.

questions.stem: A manager replicating a $20.53 million 10-year Treasury exposure with a basis point value (BPV) of $18,524 uses bond futures whose cheapest-to-deliver bond has a BPV of $88.40 per $100,000 contract and a conversion factor of 0.684. The number of futures contracts the manager must buy is closest to:

options.A: 20 contracts.
options.B: 500 contracts.

rationales.A: Far too few for the required BPV replication. At a futures BPV of $129.24 per contract, 20 contracts deliver roughly $2,585 of BPV against the $18,524 needed.
rationales.B: Too many by close to an order of magnitude. At $129.24 of BPV per contract, 500 contracts would deliver about $64,620 of BPV, well beyond the $18,524 required.
rationales.C: With the CTD a Treasury bond priced at par with 9.5 years remaining, a modified duration of 8.84 and a conversion factor of 0.684, each $100,000 futures contract has a BPV of $129.24 = $88.40/0.684. Dividing the position's BPV by the contract BPV, $18,524 / $129.24, gives approximately 143 futures contracts to replicate the $20.53 million exposure. The futures position involves initial margin plus margin movements from mark-to-market changes rather than a full principal investment.

questions.stem: The basis point value (BPV) of an interest rate swap is most likely:

options.A: Swap modified duration multiplied by notional, per basis point.
options.B: The swap's floating-leg market reference rate.

rationales.A: Swap BPV = ModDur_Swap × Swap Notional / 10,000, which is the swap's modified duration applied to notional and scaled to a one basis point move. The receive-fixed swap position is 'long' a fixed-rate term bond and 'short' a floating-rate bond, mimicking a long cash bond position by increasing duration, while the fixed-rate payer swap is a short duration position. The change in a swap's mark-to-market value may be approximated by multiplying swap BPV by the yield change.
rationales.B: MRR is the floating leg rate, not a measure of the swap's price sensitivity to a one basis point change in yield.
rationales.C: Notional alone does not give BPV. It must be scaled by the swap's modified duration and divided by 10,000 to express sensitivity to a one basis point move.

questions.stem: Over a six-month period in which rates fall 50 bps, a £100 million 10-year GBP receive-fixed swap pays a fixed rate of 2.8535% against a six-month MRR of 0.5925% and has a modified duration of 8.318. The swap's six-month gain is closest to:

rationales.A: Too small, because it misses the main components of the gain. Swap carry alone, at [(2.8535% − 0.5925%)/2] × £100 million, is £1,130,500, and the mark-to-market gain on a 50 bp fall in rates is larger still.
rationales.B: Too large by close to an order of magnitude relative to the sum of carry and mark-to-market gain on £100 million of notional for a 50 bp move in rates.
rationales.C: The 10-year GBP receive-fixed swap gains £5,364,760 over the six months. Swap carry is £1,130,500 = [(2.8535% − 0.5925%)/2] × £100 million, and the swap mark-to-market gain is £4,234,260, the difference between the present value of the fixed leg and the floating leg at par. That mark-to-market change can be approximated from the swap BPV: (8.318 × £100 million / 10,000) × 50 bps = £4,159,000. The cash outlay for the swap is limited to required collateral or margin rather than the full cash price of a bond. For comparison, a 10-year UK gilt with a 2.25% coupon priced at £93.947 to yield 2.9535% gains £5,462,778 over the same six months, made up of £1,125,000 of income and £4,337,779 of price appreciation. The swap gain is slightly less than the bond gain but requires far less capital.

drills.los_text: formulate a portfolio positioning strategy given forward interest rates and an interest rate view that diverges from the market view in terms of rate level, slope, and shape

questions.stem: A divergent rate level view most likely implies an expectation of:

options.A: A parallel shift in the yield curve.
options.B: No change in the yield curve.

rationales.A: A divergent rate level view implies an expectation of a parallel shift in the yield curve. For an active manager holding such a view, positioning the portfolio to increase profit as yield levels fall, by extending duration, or to minimize losses as yield levels rise, by reducing duration, is of primary importance. Both upward and downward parallel shifts fall under this view.
rationales.B: Expecting no change in the yield curve is a static rate view. A divergent view is by definition an expectation that rates will move away from what is currently priced.
rationales.C: Curvature is a view on the shape of the yield curve rather than its level, so it is not what a divergent rate level view implies.

questions.stem: A major yield curve strategy used to increase portfolio duration is least likely to be:

options.A: A cash bond purchase.
options.B: A receive-fixed swap.

rationales.A: A cash bond purchase (bullet) is one of the three strategies used to increase duration: duration is extended with longer-dated bonds, the return comes from price appreciation as YTM declines, and the downside risk is higher yield levels.
rationales.B: A receive-fixed swap is one of the three strategies used to increase duration: the return is the swap mark-to-market gain plus carry, the fixed rate less the floating rate, and the downside risk is higher swap yield levels and/or higher floating rates.
rationales.C: A short futures position reduces duration rather than increasing it, so it belongs among the strategies used to shorten duration. The three strategies used to increase duration are (1) a cash bond purchase (bullet), (2) a receive-fixed swap, and (3) a long futures position, which purchases a contract for forward bond delivery, earns the futures mark-to-market gain less margin cost, and carries downside risk from higher bond yields and/or higher margin cost.

questions.stem: The three major yield curve strategies available to reduce portfolio duration most likely include:

options.A: A cash bond sale, a pay-fixed swap, and a short futures position.
options.B: A cash bond sale alone.

rationales.A: The three strategies available to reduce portfolio duration are: (1) a cash bond sale (bullet) — reduce duration by selling bonds short or switching into shorter-dated bonds, which produces a smaller price decline as YTM increase, with the downside being lower yield levels; (2) a pay-fixed interest rate swap — as the fixed-rate payer, the portfolio earns a swap mark-to-market gain plus swap carry (MRR − fixed swap rate), with the downside being a swap MTM loss amid lower swap yields; and (3) a short futures position — sell a contract for forward bond delivery, earning a futures MTM gain less margin cost, with the downside being a futures MTM loss amid lower bond yields and/or higher margin cost. Only this choice names all three.
rationales.B: A cash bond sale (bullet) is genuinely one of the three, but it is only one of them. Selling or switching into shorter-dated bonds lowers duration so the portfolio suffers a smaller price decline as YTM increase, and the downside is the lower yield level accepted on the shorter bonds. Naming it on its own leaves out the pay-fixed swap and the short futures position, which belong to the set just as much, so it is an incomplete list.
rationales.C: A pay-fixed interest rate swap is genuinely one of the three, but it is only one of them. As the fixed-rate payer the portfolio gains on the swap mark-to-market as swap yields rise and earns carry of MRR less the fixed swap rate, with a swap MTM loss as the downside if swap yields fall. Naming it on its own leaves out the cash bond sale and the short futures position, so it is an incomplete list.

questions.curriculum_ref: Divergent Yield Level View — Exhibit 12 reduce duration

questions.stem: Two $50 million Treasury portfolios hold 2-year, 5-year, and 10-year bonds: an equally weighted index portfolio (modified duration 5.299, convexity 40.8) and a 20/20/60 weighted active portfolio (modified duration 6.79, convexity 60.8). For a 40 bp rise in all yields, the active portfolio's decline relative to the index portfolio is closest to:

options.A: $289,915 larger.
options.B: $181,197 larger.

rationales.A: For a 40 bp rise in yields, the index portfolio's %ΔPV = (−5.299 × 0.004) + [½ × 40.8 × (0.004)²] = −2.087%, and the active portfolio's %ΔPV = (−6.79 × 0.004) + [½ × 60.8 × (0.004)²] = −2.667%. The difference of −0.58% applied to $50 million is −$289,915, so the higher-duration active portfolio declines by $289,915 more than the index portfolio. This reinforces the danger of carrying higher-duration positions if the manager's rate view proves wrong.
rationales.B: $181,197 is the wrong magnitude. It corresponds to a differential of roughly 0.36% on $50 million, whereas the stated durations and convexities produce a differential of −2.667% − (−2.087%) = −0.58%, or $289,915. The duration gap alone contributes (6.79 − 5.299) × 0.004 = 0.596% and the convexity gap offsets only about 0.016% of it.
rationales.C: The direction of the comparison is reversed. The active portfolio carries the higher modified duration (6.79 versus 5.299), so for a parallel rise in yields it loses more, not less. Its greater convexity (60.8 versus 40.8) cushions only ½ × 20 × (0.004)² = 0.016% of the move, nowhere near enough to reverse the ranking.

questions.stem: A fixed-income manager taking a divergent view on the level of interest rates is most likely to favor:

options.A: Option-free bonds.
options.B: Callable bonds.

rationales.A: Most fixed-income managers taking a divergent rate level view tend to favor option-free bonds over callable bonds, because of the greater liquidity of option-free bonds. An exception arises when investors formulate portfolio positioning strategies based on expected changes in interest rate volatility. When the view is on the level of rates, an embedded option adds complexity and makes the instrument's duration shift with the very rate move the manager is trying to express, so the cleaner option-free instrument is preferred.
rationales.B: A callable bond's embedded call limits price upside as yields fall and shortens duration precisely when the manager taking a rate level view wants that duration, and callables are less liquid than comparable option-free bonds. Bonds with embedded options are selected to express a view on interest rate volatility, not a view on the level of rates.
rationales.C: Putable bonds are also option-embedded, and they are a specific choice for expressing a volatility view rather than the general preference under a rate level view. Restricting the answer to putables ignores the liquidity-driven preference for option-free bonds that applies when the divergent view is on the level of rates.

questions.curriculum_ref: Divergent Yield Level View — option-free preference

questions.stem: A duration-neutral yield curve steepener is most likely achieved by:

options.A: Buying both short- and long-term bonds in market-value-matched amounts.
options.B: Buying shorter-dated bonds and shorting longer-dated bonds.

rationales.A: Being long both the short and the long wing in market-value-matched amounts is a barbell, not a steepener. It leaves a large net positive duration and gains when yields fall rather than when slope increases, and it has no short leg to offset the long-end exposure. The steepener pairs a long shorter-dated position against a short longer-dated position sized to net zero duration.
rationales.B: Yield curve steepener strategies seek to gain from an increase in yield curve slope, that is, a greater difference between long-term and short-term YTM. This is achieved by combining a long shorter-dated bond position with a short longer-dated bond position: for example, buying the 2-year Treasury and selling the 10-year Treasury at par with position weights that give zero net portfolio duration. The portfolio gains if slope increases, whether that comes from a decline in the 2-year yield or a rise in the 10-year yield, because the long shorter-maturity leg gains as short-end rates fall, or falls less than the short longer-dated leg gains as long rates rise. The downside risk is yield curve flattening.
rationales.C: Buying only longer-dated bonds is a long-end bullet. It carries a large net positive duration rather than zero, and it loses as the curve steepens on rising long-end yields, which is the opposite of the exposure a steepener is built to take.

questions.stem: A bull steepener is most likely characterized by:

options.A: Short- and long-term yields unchanged.
options.B: Short-term yields falling by more than long-term yields.
options.C: Long-term yields rising by more than short-term yields.

rationales.A: Yields unchanged at both ends is a static view, not a steepening at all. A bull steepener requires two things at once: a rally in yields, which is the bull element, and a widening of the slope between long-term and short-term YTM.
rationales.B: Bull steepening is defined as short-term YTM falling by more than long-term YTM. It typically occurs when the monetary authority cuts benchmark rates to stimulate economic activity during a recession, which pulls the short end down faster than the long end and widens the slope. In the United Kingdom during the 2008 global financial crisis, the Bank of England cut the base rate six times from a peak of 5.75% in July 2007 to 2.00% in December 2008, and the gilt yield curve bull steepened accordingly.
rationales.C: Long-term yields rising by more than short-term yields is a bear steepener. The slope does widen, but yields rise rather than fall, which makes it a bear move rather than a bull move.

questions.curriculum_ref: Divergent Slope View — bull vs bear steepener

questions.stem: A bear steepener is most likely characterized by:

options.A: Long- and short-term yields drifting without direction.
options.B: Long-term yields falling by more than short-term yields.
options.C: Long-term yields rising by more than short-term yields.

rationales.A: A bear steepener is a directional rise in yields, with long-term YTM increasing by more than short-term YTM, usually on higher growth and inflation expectations. Yields drifting with no direction describes a stable-yield environment, which produces neither the bear element nor a reliable widening of the slope.
rationales.B: Falling yields are bull moves, not bear moves. A decline in yields that widens the slope requires short-term yields to fall by more than long-term yields, which is a bull steepener; long-term yields falling faster than short-term yields would in fact flatten the curve.
rationales.C: Bear steepening is long-term YTM rising by more than short-term YTM. It could result from a jump in long-term rates amid higher growth and inflation expectations while short-term rates remain unchanged. In that case, an analyst might expect the next central bank policy change to be a monetary tightening to curb inflation.

questions.stem: A yield curve flattener strategy is most likely to:

options.A: Be insensitive to changes in the curve's slope.
options.B: Combine a short short-term position with a long long-term position.
options.C: Gain from an increase in the curve's slope.

rationales.A: Sensitivity to the slope of the curve is the entire purpose of the trade. The flattener deliberately shorts the short end and goes long the long end in order to profit when the difference between long-term and short-term YTM narrows, so insensitivity to slope would mean the position does nothing at all.
rationales.B: Flattener strategies reverse the exposure profile of a steepener: a short short-term bond position and a long long-term bond position, often structured as a barbell. The gain comes from an anticipated narrowing of the difference between long-term and short-term YTM. Two variations exist: bear flattening, where short-term rates rise, and bull flattening, where long-term rates fall, often in a flight to quality. A flattener may be structured duration-neutral, net long duration in the bull flattener case, or net short duration in the bear flattener case.
rationales.C: Gaining from an increase in slope is the steepener's objective, not the flattener's. A flattener profits when the slope decreases, so this reverses the trade's purpose and would describe the opposite position.

questions.stem: A yield curve butterfly strategy for curvature most likely involves:

options.A: A long bullet paired with a short barbell, or the reverse.
options.B: Equal purchases of all maturities across the curve.
options.C: Bullet exposure concentrated at a single maturity.

rationales.A: The most common yield curve curvature strategy combines a long bullet with a short barbell portfolio, or vice versa, in what is referred to as a butterfly strategy, in order to capitalize on expected yield curve shape changes. The short-term and long-term bond positions of the barbell form the wings, while the intermediate-term bullet forms the body of the butterfly. Unlike steepeners and flatteners, the investor is either long or short both a short-term and a long-term bond and enters into an intermediate-term bullet trade in the opposite direction.
rationales.B: Buying every maturity in equal amounts is a laddered portfolio, not a butterfly. A ladder spreads exposure evenly and takes no view on curvature at all, whereas the butterfly is deliberately long the bullet and short the barbell, or the reverse, in order to profit from a change in the shape of the curve.
rationales.C: A bullet concentrated at a single maturity is only the body of the trade. Without the offsetting barbell wings there is no exposure to curvature, only a duration position, and curvature is precisely what the butterfly is constructed to capture.

questions.stem: A negative butterfly strategy anticipates lower short- and long-term yields but higher medium-term yields. The active position is most likely:

options.A: Long bullet, short barbell.
options.B: Short bullet, long barbell.

rationales.A: Long bullet, short barbell is the positive butterfly. It fits the opposite view: higher short- and long-term yields together with lower medium-term yields, where the long intermediate position gains as medium-term yields fall and the short wings gain as short- and long-term yields rise.
rationales.B: A negative butterfly combines lower short- and long-term yields with higher medium-term yields, so the matching active position is short the bullet and long the barbell. The short intermediate leg profits from the expected rise in medium-term yields, while the long wings profit from the expected decline in short- and long-term yields. The positive butterfly is the mirror image: higher short- and long-term yields with lower medium-term yields call for a long bullet and a short barbell.
rationales.C: Shorting the wings contradicts the expected decline in short- and long-term yields, because those short positions would lose value as the wings rally. Only the intermediate short leg fits the stated view; the short- and long-term legs must be long.

questions.stem: A butterfly portfolio is long $110 million of 2-year bonds, short $248.3 million of 5-year bonds, and long $110 million of 10-year bonds, leaving it net short $28.3 million with duration near zero and convexity of −139.9. If the 2-year and 10-year yields each fall 25 bp while the 5-year yield rises 50 bp, the portfolio's result is closest to:

options.A: A gain of $9.0 million.
options.B: A loss of $9.0 million.

rationales.A: Working from the money durations of the three legs, the duration-based approximation is (+25 bp × $21,934) − (50 bp × −$121,170) + (+25 bp × $99,253) = $9,088,175, and the precise answer incorporating convexity is $9,038,877, or approximately $9.04 million. The 5-year yield increase of 50 bp is larger than the 25 bp declines at the 2-year and 10-year points, so the convexity impact of the short bullet position outweighs that of the long barbell. Although the portfolio is nearly duration-neutral, it gains substantially because the butterfly spread moves from −50 bp to +100 bp.
rationales.B: The sign is reversed. The portfolio is short the bullet and long the wings, so a rise in the 5-year yield alongside declines at the 2-year and 10-year points works in its favor: the short 5-year leg gains as that yield rises and the long wings gain as their yields fall. A loss of this size would require the butterfly spread to narrow instead of widening from −50 bp to +100 bp.
rationales.C: Duration-neutrality removes exposure to a parallel shift in yields, not to a change in curvature, and the move described here is distinctly non-parallel. The portfolio's convexity of −139.9, combined with its long-wings and short-body structure, converts the widening of the butterfly spread from −50 bp to +100 bp into a large gain despite a portfolio duration of approximately zero.

drills.los_text: formulate a portfolio positioning strategy based upon expected changes in interest rate volatility

questions.stem: In markets such as the United States, where a significant portion of outstanding fixed-income bonds have embedded options, investors managing volatility most likely use:

options.A: No options at all.
options.B: Stand-alone options only.

rationales.A: Options are used in these markets; the question is how the exposure is obtained. Investors reach it mainly through cash bonds that already contain embedded optionality rather than by avoiding options altogether, so claiming no options are used misstates the practice.
rationales.B: Stand-alone options on bonds do trade, but they are the less common route. Because so much of the investable universe already carries embedded optionality, investors buy the cash bond with the option inside it more often than a separately purchased option, so an exclusively stand-alone approach reverses the usual practice.
rationales.C: In markets such as the United States, where a significant portion of outstanding fixed-income bonds — asset-backed securities among them — have embedded options, investors use cash bond positions with embedded options more frequently than stand-alone options to manage volatility. As of 2019, roughly 30% of the Bloomberg Barclays US Aggregate Bond Index was securitized debt, which mostly comprises bonds with embedded options. A manager wanting volatility exposure can therefore obtain it in size simply by buying cash bonds already in the index, without transacting in the stand-alone options market.

questions.stem: With respect to the embedded option in a callable bond, the bond investor is most likely:

options.A: Short volatility.
options.B: Long the call option.

rationales.A: With a callable bond the embedded call option is owned by the issuer, who can exercise if the yield to maturity decreases. The investor has sold the issuer the right to call the bond at a fixed price and is therefore short the call and short volatility. Because the issuer calls when yields fall, the callable bond's price appreciation is capped near the call price: as yields decline the embedded call gains value and that gain accrues to the issuer, so a long position in a callable bond appreciates less than, and underperforms, a long position in an otherwise identical option-free bond.
rationales.B: The call is owned by the issuer, not the investor. The investor has written it, so the position is short the call, not long. A long call holder gains as the underlying price rises, whereas the callable bondholder's upside is truncated once the bond price reaches the call price.
rationales.C: The embedded option makes the two bonds behave differently. The callable bond's price appreciation becomes capped as yields decline, so its price-yield profile flattens above the call price while the option-free bond's keeps rising; the callable bond also prices at a lower level, and hence a higher yield, to compensate the investor for the option written.

questions.stem: A putable bond most likely leaves the bond investor:

options.A: Positioned as in a callable bond.
options.B: Short the put option.

rationales.A: The embedded options in callable and putable bonds work in opposite directions, so the two positions are not equivalent. The call is held by the issuer and truncates the investor's upside when yields fall; the put is held by the investor and cushions the downside when yields rise.
rationales.B: The put is owned by the bond investor, who chooses whether to exercise it, so the investor is long the put, not short. A short put position would lose value as yields rose and prices fell, the opposite of what the putable bondholder experiences.
rationales.C: With a putable bond the embedded put option is owned by the bond investor, who can exercise if the yield to maturity increases; the investor is long the put and long volatility, owning the right to sell the bond back to the issuer at a fixed price. As yields rise the value of the embedded put increases, partially offsetting the bond's price decline, so the putable bond's price-yield profile has a flatter downward slope than that of an otherwise identical option-free bond.

questions.stem: For an expected downward parallel shift in the yield curve, the most profitable position among callable, putable, and option-free bonds is most likely:

options.A: Long a callable bond.
options.B: Long an option-free bond.

rationales.A: A long callable bond underperforms a long option-free bond when rates fall. As the yield to maturity decreases, the value of the embedded call option increases, and the investor is short that option: price appreciation is capped near the call price, so the callable bond captures less of the downward shift than the option-free bond does.
rationales.B: For a decrease in yield to maturity, the value of the embedded call option increases and the value of the embedded put option decreases. A long position in a callable bond underperforms a long position in an option-free bond because the rise in the call's value penalizes the callable bondholder, who is short that option and whose appreciation is capped near the call price. A short position in a putable bond also underperforms: the short bond position loses as prices rise, and the embedded put the investor is short loses value as well, so there are losses on both the bond and the option. The option-free bond captures the full price appreciation of the downward shift with no option working against the holder, which makes a long option-free position the most profitable of the three.
rationales.C: Shorting a putable bond loses money when the curve shifts downward, because the bond's price rises against the short position. The simultaneous decline in the embedded put's value does not rescue the trade — the short bond and the short option both move the wrong way.

questions.stem: Effective duration and effective convexity are most likely used when:

options.A: Future bond cash flows are contingent on interest rate changes.
options.B: The bond is option-free with fixed cash flows.

rationales.A: Effective duration and effective convexity are the relevant measures when future bond cash flows are contingent upon interest rate changes — callable bonds, putable bonds and mortgage-backed securities, for example. They are computed by repricing the position under equal up and down curve shifts: EffDur = [PV_− − PV_+] / [2 × ΔCurve × PV_0] and EffCon = [PV_− + PV_+ − 2 × PV_0] / [(ΔCurve)² × PV_0], where PV_− is the value at the decreased yield, PV_+ the value at the increased yield and PV_0 the original value. Repricing under both shifts captures how the embedded option alters the cash flows, which an analytical measure built on fixed cash flows cannot do.
rationales.B: An option-free bond with fixed cash flows can be handled with modified duration and convexity, which assume the cash flows do not change when yields move. The effective measures are needed only when that assumption fails, so an option-free bond is not the condition that calls for them.
rationales.C: Widening yield spreads are a credit or liquidity phenomenon and say nothing about whether a bond's cash flows respond to interest rate changes. Spread widening therefore does not determine whether effective rather than modified measures are required.

questions.stem: Adding a long position in a purchased bond call option to a portfolio most likely:

options.A: Decreases portfolio duration.
options.B: Leaves portfolio duration unchanged.

rationales.A: Buying a call does not reduce duration. A purchased put is the position that lowers portfolio duration, because it gains value as bond prices fall and yields rise. The call has positive sensitivity to the underlying bond price, so it adds to long bond exposure rather than offsetting it.
rationales.B: An option position is not pure volatility exposure. A bond call option has positive delta with respect to the underlying bond price, so it makes a genuine contribution to portfolio duration as well as to convexity.
rationales.C: A long bond call option is the purchase of the right to take forward bond delivery, with targeted return = Max(Bond price at lower yield − Strike, 0) − Call premium. It is exercised if the bond price appreciates beyond the strike, which generally happens at a lower yield to maturity, so the position gains alongside long bond exposure and increases portfolio duration. It also adds convexity, because the payoff is asymmetric: full participation in price appreciation above the strike, with the loss limited to the premium paid.

questions.stem: A long payer swaption most likely conveys:

options.A: No interest rate exposure.
options.B: The right to receive fixed.

rationales.A: A swaption carries substantial interest rate exposure. Its payoff depends directly on where the swap rate settles relative to the strike rate, and exercising it establishes a swap position with real duration, so treating it as rate-neutral is wrong.
rationales.B: The right to receive fixed on an interest rate swap is a receiver swaption, not a payer swaption. It pays off when rates fall and increases portfolio duration, rather than benefiting from higher rates and reducing duration.
rationales.C: A long payer swaption is ownership of the right to pay fixed on an interest rate swap at a strike rate, with targeted return = Max(Swap rate − Strike rate, 0) − Swaption premium. It is exercised when the swap rate rises above the strike, so it is the option-based way to benefit from higher rates: a manager expecting rates to rise buys a payer swaption rather than entering the pay-fixed swap outright, limiting the cost of being wrong to the premium. Because pay-fixed is a short duration position, the swaption decreases portfolio duration.

questions.stem: A long receiver swaption most likely conveys:

options.A: The right to pay fixed.
options.B: The same exposure as a payer swaption.

rationales.A: The right to pay fixed on an interest rate swap is a payer swaption. It gains when the swap rate rises above the strike and decreases portfolio duration, which is the opposite of what a receiver swaption does.
rationales.B: The two are not the same instrument and their duration effects are opposite. The receiver swaption gains when rates fall and increases portfolio duration; the payer swaption gains when rates rise and decreases portfolio duration.
rationales.C: A long receiver swaption is ownership of the right to receive fixed on an interest rate swap at a strike rate, with targeted return = Max(Strike rate − Swap rate, 0) − Swaption premium. It is exercised when the swap rate falls below the strike, so it is the option-based way to benefit from lower rates. Because receive-fixed is a long duration position, the swaption increases portfolio duration.

questions.stem: For a parallel upward shift in the yield curve, the best option strategy is most likely:

options.A: Long a put option on bond futures.
options.B: Short a payer swaption.

rationales.A: With an expected upward shift in the yield curve, the manager wants to reduce portfolio duration in anticipation of lower bond prices. A long put on a bond futures contract does exactly that: as the curve shifts upward the price of the underlying bond declines below the strike and the put increases in value, so the gain on the option offsets part of the loss on the bond portfolio, while the cost of being wrong is limited to the premium paid.
rationales.B: A short payer swaption collects a premium and gains only if rates are stable or fall. If rates rise, the option is exercised against the writer, adding a loss on the swaption to the loss already suffered on the bond portfolio. It is the long payer swaption, not the short, that benefits from higher rates.
rationales.C: A long receiver swaption is the right to receive fixed and gains when rates fall. With bond prices expected to decline and the swap rate expected to sit above the strike, the manager would not exercise, so the premium would simply be lost.

questions.stem: For an expected parallel upward shift in the yield curve, the ordering of otherwise comparable callable, putable, and option-free bonds whose embedded options are deep out of the money, from least to greatest price decline, is most likely:

options.A: Putable, option-free, callable.
options.B: Putable, callable, option-free.

rationales.A: The callable bond does not decline the most. Its embedded call loses value as rates rise, and because the investor is short that option, the fall in the option's value partially offsets the bond's price decline. The option-free bond, with no offset at all, declines more than the callable bond.
rationales.B: For a putable bond, the investor holds the option to put the bond back to the issuer, and the more rates rise the more valuable that embedded option becomes; this increasing option value partially offsets the price decline. For a callable bond, the issuer holds the option to call the bond, and the more rates rise the lower the call option's value; since the investor is short that embedded option, the fall in its value also partially offsets the price decline. The margins differ, however. As rates continue rising, the embedded put rises in value more quickly at the margin as it shifts toward being in the money, while the deep out-of-the-money embedded call moves further out of the money, so the marginal impact of further rate increases on the call's value declines. The putable bond therefore declines least, the callable next, and the option-free bond — which has no embedded option to cushion the move — declines most.
rationales.C: This reverses the ranking. The putable bond declines least, because its embedded put gains value as rates rise, and the option-free bond declines most, because it has no embedded option whose change in value offsets the price loss.

drills.los_text: evaluate a portfolio's sensitivity using key rate durations of the portfolio and its benchmark

questions.stem: Key rate duration is most likely defined as:

options.A: The standard deviation of yield changes.
options.B: Portfolio sensitivity to yield changes at individual maturities.
options.C: The aggregate duration of the portfolio.

rationales.A: The standard deviation of yield changes measures interest rate volatility, which is a dispersion statistic about rates themselves. Key rate duration measures the sensitivity of portfolio value to a change in one point on the curve, so it is a price sensitivity measure, not a measure of how variable yields are.
rationales.B: Key rate duration is defined as KeyRateDur_k = -(1/PV) x (dPV / dr_k), where r_k is the kth key rate and PV is the portfolio value, so it is the percentage change in portfolio value for a change in a single maturity's yield while the other key rates are held constant. The key rate durations sum to effective duration: sum of KeyRateDur_k = EffDur. Key rate durations help identify shaping risk for a bond portfolio, that is, a portfolio's sensitivity to changes in the shape of the benchmark yield curve. By breaking a portfolio down into its individual duration components by maturity, an active manager can pinpoint and quantify key exposures along the curve.
rationales.C: Aggregate portfolio duration is the sum of the key rate durations, so it is a consequence of them rather than a definition of them. It measures the response to a parallel shift only, and because it nets offsetting exposures across maturities it hides curve-shape mismatches that the individual key rate durations reveal.

questions.stem: An index portfolio holds equal face values of $100 million each in zero-coupon US Treasuries, with market values of $98.03 million at 2 years, $90.57 million at 5 years, and $74.40 million at 10 years, for a total portfolio value of $263 million. The portfolio modified duration is closest to:

rationales.A: Each zero's yield follows from its price: (100/98.03)^(1/2) - 1 = 1.0%, (100/90.57)^(1/5) - 1 = 2.0%, and (100/74.40)^(1/10) - 1 = 3.0%. For a zero-coupon bond, Macaulay duration equals maturity, so modified duration is 2/1.01 = 1.980, 5/1.02 = 4.902, and 10/1.03 = 9.709. Weighting each by its share of market value gives Portfolio ModDur = [1.98 x (98.03/263)] + [4.902 x (90.57/263)] + [9.709 x (74.40/263)] = 0.738 + 1.688 + 2.747 = 5.173. Those three contributions are the key rate durations themselves, and their sum confirms that the key rate durations add up to effective duration.
rationales.B: 9.71 is the modified duration of the 10-year zero taken on its own. That bond is only 74.40/263 = 28.3% of portfolio value, so it contributes 9.709 x 0.283 = 2.747 to portfolio duration, not 9.709. Using the longest holding's duration as the portfolio's duration ignores the market value weights.
rationales.C: 1.98 is the modified duration of the 2-year zero taken on its own. Its weight of 98.03/263 = 37.3% means it contributes only 1.98 x 0.373 = 0.738 to portfolio duration, with the 5-year and 10-year holdings supplying the remaining 4.435.

questions.stem: An active portfolio holds zero-coupon US Treasuries with position values of $51.4 million at 2 years, short $46 million at 5 years, and $257.6 million at 10 years, for a total portfolio value of $263 million. Given modified durations of 1.980, 4.902, and 9.709 at those three maturities, the portfolio modified duration is closest to:

rationales.A: A mix of long and short positions is not automatically duration neutral. The negative contribution from the short 5-year position is far smaller than the positive contributions from the long 2-year and 10-year positions, so the portfolio retains substantial interest rate exposure rather than netting to zero.
rationales.B: Weight each modified duration by the position's share of portfolio value, carrying the short position through with a negative weight: Active Portfolio ModDur = [1.98 x (51.4/263)] + [4.902 x (-46/263)] + [9.709 x (257.6/263)] = 0.387 - 0.857 + 9.509 = 9.039. The three terms are the key rate durations: the long 2-year position contributes 0.387, the short 5-year position a negative 4.902 x (-46/263) = -0.857, and the long 10-year position 9.509. The resulting profile, short the middle of the curve and heavily long the long end, positions the manager for a combination of a negative butterfly and a bull flattening at the long end of the yield curve.
rationales.C: 5.173 is the modified duration of the equally weighted index portfolio of the same three zeros, not of this active portfolio. Concentrating value in the 10-year zero and shorting the 5-year raises the active portfolio's duration well above the index's, which is why a duration comparison alone flags the position as long duration without showing where along the curve the exposure sits.

questions.stem: An active portfolio's key rate durations, against its index portfolio's, are 0.39 versus 0.74 at 2 years, -0.86 versus 1.69 at 5 years, and 9.51 versus 2.75 at 10 years. The active portfolio is most likely:

options.A: Matched to the index at every maturity.
options.B: Underexposed to 10-year yield changes.
options.C: Underexposed to short rates and overexposed to 10-year yields.

rationales.A: The tenor-by-tenor differences are large, not negligible: -0.35 at 2 years, -2.55 at 5 years, and +6.76 at 10 years. A portfolio matched to its index would show key rate durations close to the index's at each maturity, which is plainly not the case here.
rationales.B: The 10-year difference is +6.76 (9.51 versus 2.75), so the active portfolio's exposure to 10-year yield changes is far greater than the index's, not lower. The underexposures sit at the 2-year and 5-year tenors.
rationales.C: The negative differences for the 2-year and 5-year maturities (-0.35 and -2.55, respectively) indicate that the active portfolio has lower exposure to short-term rates than the index portfolio. The large positive difference in the 10-year tenor (+6.76) shows that the active portfolio has far greater exposure to 10-year yield-to-maturity changes. Reading the key rate durations maturity by maturity in this way supplies information that a comparison of the two portfolios' aggregate durations cannot, because the aggregate statistic nets the short middle against the long end and conceals where the active risk is being taken.

questions.stem: Regarding the information content of aggregate portfolio duration and key rate durations, the most likely accurate statement is that:

options.A: aggregate duration captures all of a portfolio's shaping risk.
options.B: aggregate duration cannot capture non-parallel yield curve shifts.
options.C: key rate durations serve only to verify aggregate duration.

rationales.A: Aggregate portfolio duration measures sensitivity to a parallel shift and nets offsetting exposures across maturities, so it conceals shaping risk rather than capturing it. Two portfolios with identical aggregate duration can hold very different exposures along the curve and perform very differently when the curve steepens, flattens, or twists.
rationales.B: Aggregate portfolio duration cannot capture how a portfolio responds to non-parallel yield curve shifts. A comparison of the active versus index portfolio duration summary statistic does not tell the entire story; instead, comparing the key rate, or partial, durations for specific maturities across the index and active portfolios gives a better understanding of exposure differences. Key rate durations identify the specific maturity points at which a portfolio deviates from its benchmark, which is precisely the information needed when rates at different maturities move by different amounts.
rationales.C: Key rate durations do sum to effective duration, so they are consistent with the aggregate figure, but their purpose is to supply the detail the aggregate figure lacks: the distribution of interest rate exposure across maturities, and hence the portfolio's shaping risk. Treating them as a check on aggregate duration discards the exposure information they were constructed to show.

questions.stem: An active manager's key rate duration differences versus the index bond portfolio are -2.821 at 5 years, -0.291 at 10 years, and +2.933 at 30 years, with a portfolio modified duration difference of -0.179. Using only derivatives overlaid on the index bond portfolio, the manager's positions are most likely:

options.A: Receive-fixed 5y swap, short 10y futures, pay-fixed 30y swap.
options.B: Pay-fixed 5y swap, short 10y futures, receive-fixed 30y swap.
options.C: Short 5y futures, long 10y futures, receive-fixed 30y swap.

rationales.A: A receive-fixed swap is long duration at its tenor, so a receive-fixed 5-year swap would add 5-year key rate duration and produce a positive difference versus the index. The manager's 5-year difference is -2.821, a short exposure, so the 5-year leg has to shed duration. The 30-year leg is wrong for the same reason in reverse: a pay-fixed 30-year swap is short duration at 30 years, the opposite of the +2.933 difference.
rationales.B: The key rate duration differences show the manager net short 5-year and 10-year exposure and net long 30-year exposure versus the index. A pay-fixed 5-year swap is short duration at 5 years, matching the -2.821 difference. Short 10-year futures are short duration at 10 years, matching the small -0.291 difference. A receive-fixed 30-year swap is long duration at 30 years, matching the +2.933 difference. Summed, these overlays leave the portfolio modified duration difference slightly negative at -0.179, so the position is close to duration neutral and expresses a view on the shape of the curve rather than on its level.
rationales.C: Long 10-year futures are long duration at 10 years and would give a positive 10-year key rate duration difference, whereas the manager's 10-year difference is -0.291, a small short exposure. The short 5-year futures and the receive-fixed 30-year swap do carry the right signs, but the 10-year leg is reversed, so this combination cannot produce the observed differences.

questions.stem: Shaping risk is most likely defined as:

options.A: A portfolio's sensitivity to the shape of the benchmark yield curve.
options.B: The risk that a manager reshapes the portfolio.
options.C: A portfolio's sensitivity to parallel shifts alone.

rationales.A: In contrast to effective duration, key rate durations help identify shaping risk for a bond portfolio, that is, a portfolio's sensitivity to changes in the shape of the benchmark yield curve. By breaking down a portfolio into its individual duration components by maturity, an active manager can pinpoint and quantify key exposures along the curve, and can compare them with the benchmark's tenor by tenor.
rationales.B: Shaping risk has nothing to do with manager behaviour, portfolio turnover, or a mandate being rewritten. The shape in question is the shape of the yield curve, and the risk is measured by the portfolio's key rate durations at specific maturities.
rationales.C: Sensitivity to a parallel shift is what effective duration measures, and it is the exposure that remains after the parallel component is stripped out that constitutes shaping risk: the response to steepening, flattening, and twisting of the curve, which a single duration statistic cannot describe.

questions.stem: A short position in a given maturity bucket most likely produces:

options.A: A negative key rate duration contribution.
options.B: A positive key rate duration contribution.

rationales.A: A key rate duration contribution is the position's modified duration multiplied by the position's share of portfolio value, so a negative position value produces a negative contribution. In the active zero-coupon Treasury portfolio, the short $46 million 5-year position has a key rate duration of 4.902 x (-46/263) = -0.857. Negative contributions are what allow an active manager to express an explicit short view on one part of the yield curve while remaining long elsewhere, and they are why a long-short portfolio's key rate durations can offset one another.
rationales.B: Positive contributions come from long positions, where the market value weight is positive. Shorting flips the sign of that weight while leaving the instrument's modified duration positive, so the product is negative: the short 5-year position contributes 4.902 x (-46/263) = -0.857, not +0.857.
rationales.C: Key rate duration is defined for any rate-sensitive position, short as well as long, because it depends only on modified duration and the position's share of portfolio value. The short 5-year position's key rate duration of 4.902 x (-46/263) = -0.857 is a real exposure that must be counted; dropping shorts from the calculation would overstate the portfolio's duration at that tenor.

questions.stem: Beyond zero-coupon bonds, key rate duration analysis most likely applies to:

options.A: Government securities only.
options.B: Fixed-coupon bonds, swaps, and other rate-sensitive instruments.

rationales.A: Key rate durations are stated at benchmark par maturities, which is why government yields serve as the reference points, but the measure is not confined to government securities. Swaps, futures, and credit instruments all have modified durations at those tenors and can be weighted into the same analysis.
rationales.B: A simple zero-coupon bond example may be extended to portfolios consisting of fixed-coupon bonds, swaps, and other rate-sensitive instruments that may be included in a fixed-income portfolio. In practice an active manager overlays 5-year, 10-year, and 30-year swaps and futures on an index bond portfolio and reads the resulting key rate duration differences maturity by maturity, exactly as with the zero-coupon holdings; a pay-fixed swap or short futures position simply enters with a negative duration contribution at its tenor.
rationales.C: Key rate durations can be computed for instruments with embedded options by taking effective durations from a pricing model that reprices the contingent cash flows under each shifted key rate, so the extension is not limited to option-free cash flows. Callable and mortgage-backed exposures are in fact among the main reasons to look at key rate durations rather than a single duration number.

questions.stem: An active manager is net long 30-year key rate duration by +2.933 versus the index, net short 5-year by -2.821, and net short 10-year by -0.291. The portfolio most likely reflects:

options.A: A positive butterfly view.
options.B: A bear steepening view.

rationales.A: A butterfly position is a view on the middle of the curve against both wings, taken by going long the belly and short the wings, or the reverse. This manager is long one wing, the 30-year, and short the 5-year and 10-year tenors, which is a directional view on the long end rather than a curvature trade.
rationales.B: A bear steepening is a rise in long-term yields by more than short-term yields. A manager expecting that would shorten duration at the long end of the curve, so the +2.933 long 30-year key rate duration is the opposite of the position the view would call for.
rationales.C: Being net long 30-year key rate duration while net short the 5-year and 10-year tenors is consistent with a bull flattening view: the manager expects long-term yields to fall by more than short-term yields, or short-term yields to rise while long-term yields fall. The long 30-year exposure captures the price gain as long yields decline, while the short 5-year and 10-year exposures, taken through a pay-fixed swap and short futures on the shorter tenors, limit the loss if yields at those maturities rise. With the portfolio modified duration difference only -0.179, the position is close to duration neutral, so the return comes from the change in the curve's shape rather than from its level. Bull flattening is common in flight-to-quality environments.
