questions.stem: For a foreign-currency bond position, the domestic-currency return is most likely:

options.A: the compounded combination of the foreign-currency return and the FX return.
options.B: the product of the foreign-currency return and the FX return.
options.C: the sum of the foreign-currency return and the FX return.

rationales.A: For a single asset, R_DC = (1 + R_FC)(1 + R_FX) − 1. For a portfolio, R_DC = Σ ω_i (1 + R_FC,i)(1 + R_FX,i) − 1, where R_DC and R_FC are the domestic- and foreign-currency returns, R_FX is the percentage change in the value of the domestic versus the foreign currency, and the ω_i are portfolio weights summing to 1. The relationship is multiplicative in gross returns rather than additive in net returns: the cross-product R_FC × R_FX is the interaction between the bond's local return and the currency move, and it is exactly what a simple sum omits. This expression combines two of the components of expected fixed-income return — the expected price change from the manager's view of benchmark yields, and the expected price change from the manager's view of currency value changes.
rationales.B: Multiplying the two net returns together, R_FC × R_FX, is not the compounding relationship. The product of net returns is a second-order interaction term, not the total return: it would give a near-zero result whenever either component return is small, and exactly zero whenever either is zero, even though the other leg still contributes its full return. Compounding multiplies the gross returns, (1 + R_FC)(1 + R_FX), and then subtracts 1, so the product of the net returns is only one of the three pieces of the answer.
rationales.C: The simple sum, R_FC + R_FX, drops the cross-term. Expanding the compounded form gives R_DC = (1 + R_FC)(1 + R_FX) − 1 = R_FC + R_FX + (R_FC × R_FX), so the sum misstates the domestic-currency return by exactly the product of the two component returns. The approximation is tolerable only for small returns over short horizons; for large currency moves or long holding periods the omitted interaction term is material, and it is signed — it adds to the return when both components move the same way and subtracts when they move in opposite directions.

questions.stem: Covered interest rate parity most likely establishes:

options.A: no link between the forward and spot exchange rates.
options.B: a forward rate scaled by the ratio of the two risk-free rates.
options.C: a forward rate equal to the spot rate in all circumstances.

rationales.A: Covered interest rate parity defines the relationship between spot and forward rates precisely, through the interest rate differential: the forward rate is pinned to the spot rate by the ratio of the gross domestic and foreign risk-free rates over the horizon. If no such relationship held, a fully hedged foreign investment could earn more or less than the domestic risk-free rate, and a riskless arbitrage would be available by borrowing in one market, investing in the other, and locking in the conversion with a forward.
rationales.B: F(DC/FC, T) = S_0(DC/FC) × [(1 + r_DC)^T / (1 + r_FC)^T], where F is the T-period forward rate, S_0 the spot rate, and r_DC and r_FC the domestic and foreign risk-free rates. The relationship is an arbitrage condition: an investor who uses a forward contract to fully hedge foreign-currency cash flows should expect to earn the domestic risk-free rate, no more and no less. It follows that a higher-yielding currency trades at a forward discount while a lower-yielding currency trades at a forward premium, because the forward price has to give back the interest advantage. A spot rate of 1.1218 against a 2-year forward of 1.187 is consistent with USD rates above EUR rates in 2019.
rationales.C: The forward rate equals the spot rate only in the special case where the two risk-free rates are equal, which makes the ratio (1 + r_DC)^T / (1 + r_FC)^T equal to one. In general F = S_0 × (1 + r_DC)^T / (1 + r_FC)^T, so any interest rate differential drives the forward away from spot, and the gap widens with the horizon T. The higher-yielding currency trades at a forward discount and the lower-yielding currency at a forward premium; a forward permanently equal to spot would let an investor hedge into the higher rate and earn it risk-free.

questions.stem: Uncovered interest rate parity most likely suggests that:

options.A: unhedged and domestic exposure earn the same return over time.
options.B: unhedged exposure always outperforms domestic exposure.
options.C: hedged exposure always outperforms unhedged exposure.

rationales.A: Uncovered interest rate parity holds that over time the return on unhedged foreign-currency exposure will be the same as the return on a domestic-currency investment: the interest rate advantage of the higher-yielding currency is expected to be offset by depreciation of that currency. Forward FX rates should therefore in theory be an unbiased predictor of future spot FX rates. In practice, investors sometimes seek to exploit a persistent divergence from interest rate parity conditions, known as the forward rate bias, by investing in higher-yielding currencies — sometimes enhanced by borrowing in lower-yielding currencies, which is the carry trade.
rationales.B: Higher-yielding currencies have historically delivered excess returns to unhedged investors, but that is a persistent empirical bias — the forward rate bias that carry traders try to harvest — and not a theorem. Uncovered interest rate parity says the opposite: the yield advantage is expected to be given back through currency depreciation, so unhedged exposure earns the domestic return on average. Carry trades do best in stable, low-volatility markets, and the premium can reverse sharply when the funding currency appreciates.
rationales.C: Hedging removes currency risk, and by covered interest rate parity it converts the foreign investment into the domestic risk-free rate; it does not deliver systematically higher returns. There is a trade-off in both directions: the hedge surrenders any favorable currency move and costs the interest rate differential embedded in the forward points, so a hedged position underperforms an unhedged one whenever the foreign currency appreciates, or simply fails to depreciate by as much as the forward implied.

questions.stem: A cross-currency carry trade is an extension of the single-currency repo carry: an investor borrows short-term in one currency and most likely invests in:

options.A: A higher-yielding foreign currency.
options.B: A domestic bond.

rationales.A: The cross-currency carry trade extends the single-currency repo carry trade: the investor borrows short-term in one currency and invests in another, higher-yielding currency. A European fixed-income manager buying a 2-year US Treasury zero-coupon bond, for instance, might use leverage instead of cash by borrowing in euros. The positive interest rate differential is a potential source of additional income, subject to short-term funding availability, if that differential persists for the life of the transaction. Because the position is unhedged, it carries the foreign yield curve risk and the currency risk alongside the rollover risk on the borrowing.
rationales.B: Buying a domestic bond with domestic short-term borrowing is a single-currency carry trade, not a cross-currency one. The cross-currency version is defined by its two legs being denominated in different currencies: the income comes from the interest rate differential between the funding currency and the investment currency, and that differential does not exist when both legs sit in the same market, where only the term spread is available.
rationales.C: Borrowing short-term and buying a short-term bill in the same currency is same-currency financing — repo-style carry at best, and with matched maturities no carry at all. It leaves no interest rate differential across currencies to earn, so it is not the cross-currency carry trade; that trade requires the invested currency to be a different, higher-yielding one, which is also what introduces the exchange rate risk the carry is compensation for.

questions.stem: An investor borrows for one year in USD at 1.85% and invests the proceeds in 90-day MXN T-bills yielding 7.70% annualized, rolling them over at a stable MXN/USD rate of 19.15. The expected profit on the trade is closest to:

rationales.A: Too high. A 10% figure exceeds even the gross MXN T-bill yield of 7.70% annualized, and the carry trade earns only the differential between the MXN investment yield and the USD funding cost, never the gross investment yield. Compounding the 90-day MXN rate quarterly lifts the MXN leg to about 7.93% for the year, and subtracting the 1.85% gross cost of the one-year USD loan leaves roughly 6.08%.
rationales.B: Too low. A figure near 0.50% would be right only if the two rates were nearly equal, but here the 90-day MXN bill pays 7.70% annualized against a 1.85% USD borrowing cost — a differential of close to six percentage points. Expected carry trade profit = (1 + 0.077/4)^4 − (1 + 0.0185) ≈ 6.08%.
rationales.C: Expected carry trade profit = (1 + 0.077/4)^4 − (1 + 0.0185) ≈ 6.08%. The first term compounds the 90-day MXN yield quarterly, since the investor rolls the T-bill four times over the year, giving a gross MXN return of about 1.0793; the second term is the gross cost of the one-year USD loan, 1.0185. The difference, about 6.08%, is the annualized carry. It assumes that 90-day MXN rates and the MXN/USD exchange rate both remain stable over the year, so it is an expected rather than a locked-in return: the position is unhedged, and either a change in MXN yields at each rollover or peso depreciation would move the realized figure away from 6.08%.

questions.stem: A one-year cross-currency carry trade funded in USD and invested in rolling 90-day MXN T-bills realizes about 3.61% rather than the 6.08% expected at inception. This is most likely because:

options.A: MXN yields fell over the horizon.
options.B: The USD funding rate changed over the horizon.
options.C: MXN yields rose and the peso depreciated.

rationales.A: The 90-day MXN yields rose over the horizon rather than falling, from 7.70% at inception to 8.20% by day 270, so the shortfall cannot be attributed to a decline in Mexican rates. Higher yields raise the income earned on each bill bought at rollover, which works in the investor's favor on the investment leg; what actually undercut the trade was the late-period depreciation of the peso, from 19.15 to 19.65 MXN/USD, which converted the MXN proceeds back into fewer dollars at the end.
rationales.B: The USD borrowing cost was fixed when the one-year loan was taken down at 1.85%, so no subsequent change in USD funding rates could affect this trade's realized return. The drag came from the investment and currency legs instead: the 90-day MXN yields moved as the bills were rolled, and the peso depreciated against the dollar from 19.15 to 19.65 MXN/USD. Fixing the funding leg for the full horizon is precisely what removes funding-rate risk from this structure, leaving reinvestment and FX risk behind.
rationales.C: Over the horizon the 90-day MXN yields rose, from 7.70% at inception to 8.20% at 270 days, and the peso depreciated slightly against the dollar by year-end, from 19.15 to 19.65 MXN/USD. Rolling the trade over for the full 12 months produced a realized return of about 3.61% against the 6.08% expected. The trade was ultimately profitable but was exposed to risk throughout: despite the rise in 90-day MXN yields, a late-period peso depreciation undercut the profitability of the trade, because the MXN proceeds converted back into fewer dollars than the stable-FX assumption implied. Carry trades are unhedged by construction and are most successful in stable, low-volatility markets.

questions.stem: A German investor buys a 2-year US Treasury zero-coupon bond and fully hedges the dollar exposure with a 2-year currency forward. The annualized EUR return received is most likely:

options.A: above the US Treasury yield.
options.B: equal to the 2-year German government zero-coupon yield.

rationales.A: The forward hedge locks in the domestic risk-free rate, not a return above the US Treasury yield. Covered interest rate parity prices the forward so that the US yield advantage is given back through the forward points: the dollar, as the higher-yielding currency, trades at a forward discount, and converting the hedged dollar proceeds back into euros surrenders exactly the interest rate differential. A fully hedged investor therefore cannot capture the higher US yield at all; the only way to earn it is to leave the currency exposure unhedged and bear the FX risk.
rationales.B: The expected annualized EUR return on the fully hedged 2-year US Treasury zero-coupon investment is about −0.60%, computed as (€84,245,998/€85,270,102)^0.5 − 1, which matches the 2-year annualized German government zero-coupon yield-to-maturity at inception. This is covered interest rate parity in practice: hedging away the FX risk converts the foreign investment into the domestic risk-free rate, so the German investor ends up earning the German zero-coupon yield regardless of the higher yield on the US Treasury bond actually held.
rationales.C: The hedged EUR return is negative, not zero, because the 2-year German zero-coupon yield it reproduces was itself about −0.60% at inception. A zero result would require the domestic risk-free rate to be zero. Hedging converts the US Treasury position into the domestic risk-free rate whatever that rate happens to be, and in a negative-yield EUR environment that means a small negative annualized return — the investor pays, in effect, for the certainty.

questions.stem: Cross-currency basis is most likely defined as:

options.A: the gap between direct and synthetic USD funding rates.
options.B: the gap between EUR and USD policy rates.
options.C: a gap that arbitrage always closes to zero.

rationales.A: The basis, or spread, shown in a cross-currency basis swap is the difference between the direct USD interest rate and the synthetic USD interest rate derived from swapping another currency, such as JPY, into US dollars. A positive (negative) currency basis means the direct USD interest rate is higher (lower) than the synthetic USD interest rate. Covered interest rate parity suggests the cross-currency basis should be close to zero, but the JPY and EUR cross-currency basis was persistently negative following the 2008 global financial crisis. Du, Tepper, and Verdelhan (2018) attribute this to higher post-2008 financial intermediation costs and international imbalances.
rationales.B: The basis is not a policy rate differential. It is the gap between direct USD funding and the synthetic USD funding created by swapping another currency, such as JPY or EUR, into dollars. Policy rate differentials are already embedded in both legs and in the forward points that link them, so a difference between two central banks' target rates implies nothing about the basis. The basis is what remains after the interest rate differential has been accounted for: it measures the breakdown of covered interest rate parity rather than the differential itself, and it can be non-zero even when the two policy rates are identical.
rationales.C: A persistently non-zero basis is well documented: the JPY and EUR cross-currency basis stayed negative for years following the 2008 global financial crisis, even though covered interest rate parity suggests it should be close to zero. Post-crisis funding frictions — higher financial intermediation costs, constrained dealer balance sheets, and international imbalances — keep arbitrage from closing the gap. Because the basis is not always zero, it is a real cost or benefit to a cross-currency investor hedging with swaps or forwards.

questions.stem: An active cross-currency yield curve strategy faces three potential risks. These are most likely:

options.A: curve moves in both currencies and exchange rate changes.
options.B: exchange rate changes only.
options.C: curve moves in one currency only.

rationales.A: The resulting yield curve strategy faces three potential risks: yield curve movements — level, slope, or curvature — in the overweight currency; yield curve changes in the underweight currency; and exchange rate changes. All three are live because the position is overweight duration in one market, underweight duration in another, and exposed across the two currencies. An active cross-currency yield curve strategy must therefore combine a view on currency appreciation versus depreciation with views on how each country's curve will shift and twist.
rationales.B: Exchange rate changes are only one of the three risks. Interest rate risk is present in both currencies: an adverse level, slope, or curvature move in the overweight market hurts the long leg, and an adverse move in the underweight market hurts the underweight leg. Treating the position as a pure currency bet ignores the two yield curve exposures that generate most of its tracking error, and those exposures can swamp the currency result over short horizons.
rationales.C: Interest rate risk in a single currency understates the exposure. Both currencies' yield curves are at risk — the overweight market through its own level, slope, and curvature moves, and the underweight market through its — and the exchange rate between them is a third, separate source of risk, since the return earned on the foreign leg has to be converted back into the domestic currency before it is realized.

questions.stem: A manager expects bear flattening in a higher-yielding foreign currency market, where short-term yields rise more than long-term yields, alongside a stable, upward-sloping domestic curve. The strategy generating the largest carry benefit is most likely to:

options.A: receive fixed in foreign and pay fixed in domestic.
options.B: receive fixed in foreign and pay floating in domestic.
options.C: receive floating in foreign and pay floating in domestic.

rationales.A: Receiving fixed in the foreign currency misses the bear flattening. If foreign short-term yield-to-maturity rises by more than long-term yield-to-maturity, a receive-fixed leg is locked into the long-term rate that barely moves while the manager pays away the rising short-term rate, so the position fails to benefit from the expected shift. Paying fixed in the domestic currency compounds the problem by giving up the carry available from paying the low domestic floating rate on a stable, upward-sloping domestic curve.
rationales.B: The foreign leg has the same problem: receiving fixed does not capture the rise in foreign short-term yields that bear flattening produces, because the fixed rate received is set off the long end, which moves least. Paying domestic floating is the right choice on the domestic side given the stable, upward-sloping domestic curve, but the foreign leg must be receive-floating for the strategy to benefit from short-term foreign yields increasing by more than long-term foreign yields.
rationales.C: If the higher-yielding foreign currency experiences a bear flattening in the yield curve as the manager expects, foreign currency short-term yield-to-maturity will increase by more than long-term yield-to-maturity, so she will want to receive floating in the foreign currency and capture those rising short-term yields at each reset. Given the upward-sloping domestic yield curve, domestic floating rates sit at the low end of that curve, so the carry difference between receiving foreign currency floating rates and paying domestic currency floating rates would be expected to be the highest of the available combinations.

questions.stem: Scenario analysis of a fixed-income portfolio is most likely described as:

options.A: Changing one variable at a time.
options.B: Changing multiple assumptions at once.

rationales.A: Moving a single variable while holding everything else fixed is sensitivity analysis, not scenario analysis. It isolates the effect of one input and therefore cannot capture the joint impact of correlated moves in rates and currencies, which is precisely what scenario analysis is built to measure.
rationales.B: Scenario analysis involves changing multiple assumptions at once to assess the overall impact of unexpected market changes on a portfolio's value. Managers may apply historical rate and currency changes or construct specific stress tests within the same framework. For instance, a leveraged investor might evaluate how far rates or currencies must move before she faces a collateral or margin call or is forced to unwind a position.
rationales.C: Historical rate and currency changes are only one source of scenarios. Managers also build user-defined stress tests, so restricting the exercise to historical inputs would understate the range of outcomes a portfolio can face and would miss shocks with no historical precedent.

questions.stem: Portfolio A holds only a 5-year Treasury, and Portfolio B is a barbell of 58.94% 2-year and 41.06% 10-year Treasuries. Both have an effective duration of 4.88. Under a bear steepening in which the 5-year yield rises 50 bp and the 10-year yield rises 100 bp, the most likely outcome is:

options.A: Both portfolios lose equally.
options.B: Both portfolios gain.
options.C: Portfolio B loses more than Portfolio A.

rationales.A: Equal effective duration of 4.88 makes the two portfolios respond alike to a parallel shift, but a steepening is not a parallel shift. Portfolio B's 41.06% weight in the 10-year note absorbs the full 100 bp rise at the long end, while Portfolio A's single 5-year holding sees only 50 bp, so the losses are 2.407% for Portfolio A against 3.518% for Portfolio B rather than the same amount.
rationales.B: A bear steepening raises yields at both points on the curve, so both portfolios fall in price; a gain would require yields to decline. The mirror-image bull flattening of 5-year minus 50 bp and 10-year minus 100 bp is the scenario that produces gains, of 2.473% for Portfolio A and 3.891% for Portfolio B.
rationales.C: Applying each portfolio's exposures to the scenario gives Portfolio A minus 2.407%, a $1,203,437 loss, and Portfolio B minus 3.518%, a $1,759,216 loss. Portfolio B loses more because its 41.06% long-end weight takes the full 100 bp rise in the 10-year yield, while Portfolio A's 5-year position takes only 50 bp. Under the bull flattening the ranking reverses in sign: Portfolio A gains 2.473% ($1,236,563) and Portfolio B gains 3.891% ($1,945,628). Identical duration makes the two behave alike under parallel shifts and very differently once the slope of the curve moves, which is the central limitation of judging risk by duration alone.

questions.curriculum_ref: Framework for Evaluating YC Strategies — Example 14

questions.stem: Portfolio A holds only a 5-year Treasury, and Portfolio B is a duration-matched barbell of 2-year and 10-year Treasuries with 41.06% at the long end. Under a bull flattening in which the 5-year yield falls 50 bp and the 10-year yield falls 100 bp, Portfolio B's gain is most likely:

options.A: Smaller than Portfolio A's.
options.B: Zero.

rationales.A: The gain of 2.473%, or $1,236,563, belongs to Portfolio A, the single 5-year holding, which captures only the 50 bp decline. Portfolio B's 41.06% weight in the 10-year note captures the full 100 bp rally at the long end, so its gain of 3.891%, or $1,945,628, exceeds Portfolio A's rather than falling short of it.
rationales.B: A barbell is not immune to curve changes. Its long-end leg leaves it heavily exposed to the 10-year yield, so a 100 bp decline there delivers the larger of the two gains, not an absence of gain. Immunity to curve movements would require matched exposure at every key rate, which a two-point barbell against a single 5-year bullet does not have.
rationales.C: Under the bull flattening Portfolio A gains 2.473% ($1,236,563) while Portfolio B gains 3.891% ($1,945,628). Portfolio B's larger gain reflects its 41.06% weight in the 10-year Treasury, which experiences the 100 bp yield decline, against Portfolio A's exposure to only the 50 bp decline in the 5-year. Both portfolios carry an effective duration of 4.88, so this is a direct demonstration that duration-matched portfolios can perform very differently once the slope of the curve changes.

questions.curriculum_ref: Framework for Evaluating YC Strategies — bull flattening

questions.stem: Under a parallel shift in the yield curve, two portfolios of similar effective duration will most likely:

options.A: Perform identically.
options.B: Perform similarly, apart from a convexity difference.

rationales.A: Matching duration aligns the first-order price response but not the second. A duration-matched barbell with convexity of 40.229 against a bullet's 26.5 gains slightly more when rates fall and loses slightly less when they rise by the same amount, so performance is close rather than identical.
rationales.B: Portfolios of similar duration perform similarly under a parallel shift, with the residual gap coming from their convexity difference. With both at a duration of about 4.88, the barbell's higher convexity of 40.229 against 26.5 means it gains slightly more on a rate decline and loses slightly less on a rate rise of the same size. This is one of the key limitations of using duration alone to gauge portfolio risk: the equivalence holds only for parallel shifts, and under changes in the slope or shape of the curve the same two portfolios perform very differently.
rationales.C: Large divergences between duration-matched portfolios come from changes in the slope or shape of the curve, not from a parallel shift. A bear steepening, for example, separates a 5-year bullet's 2.407% loss from a 2-year and 10-year barbell's 3.518% loss, but a level shift leaves only the convexity difference.

questions.curriculum_ref: Framework for Evaluating YC Strategies — parallel shift comparison

questions.stem: A US manager comparing an AUD bullet with an AUD barbell over a one-year horizon forecasts a 60 bp downward parallel shift in the Australian zero-coupon yield curve and 0.25% appreciation of the AUD against the USD. Both structures have an average price today of $98 and an expected effective duration in one year of 3.95. Evaluating the trade most likely requires:

options.A: The currency forecast only.
options.B: No distinction between the two structures.
options.C: Rolldown, duration, and currency returns combined.

rationales.A: Both legs of the trade matter. The 0.25% currency gain is small next to the price response to a 60 bp decline against a duration of 3.95, which is roughly 2.37%, and the currency view says nothing at all about the rolldown difference between a bullet and a barbell. A view on the AUD alone cannot rank the two structures.
rationales.B: The bullet and the barbell respond differently to the same 60 bp parallel shift because their convexity and rolldown profiles differ. Under an unchanged curve the bullet's expected end-of-horizon price is 99.75 against the barbell's 100.00, so their rolldown returns already diverge before any curve or currency effect is added, and the comparison is therefore not moot.
rationales.C: The expected return combines, first, rolldown return, with the bullet rolling to an expected end-of-horizon price of 99.75 against the barbell's 100.00 under a stable curve, so the two roll down by different amounts; second, the duration-based price response to the 60 bp parallel decline, approximately 60 bp times 3.95, or about 2.37%; third, any convexity contribution; and fourth, the currency return of 0.25%. The expected AUD total return is then translated into US dollars as R_DC = (1 + R_FC)(1 + R_FX) - 1. Every element of the expected-return decomposition thus contributes, and the framework for a single-currency portfolio extends to the cross-currency case through that conversion.

questions.curriculum_ref: Framework for Evaluating YC Strategies — Example 15 AUD

questions.stem: For a leveraged fixed-income investor, scenario analysis most likely evaluates:

options.A: No risks.
options.B: Expected returns only.
options.C: The rate or currency move that would trigger a margin call.

rationales.A: Risk measurement is the central purpose of the exercise. The whole point of running scenarios is to find how large an adverse move the portfolio can absorb before financing or collateral constraints bind, which is a risk question rather than a return question.
rationales.B: Scenario analysis examines downside outcomes as well as the central case. For a leveraged investor the binding question is a loss threshold, not an expected return: the position can be closed out against her by a margin call long before any expected return is realized.
rationales.C: A leveraged investor uses scenario analysis to evaluate how far rates or currencies must move before she faces a collateral or margin call or is forced to unwind a position. Fixed-income portfolio models supply a variety of historical and user-defined scenarios for exactly this purpose. The threshold matters because a forced unwind occurs at the least favorable moment, crystallizing losses and removing the position before any recovery, which can severely damage returns on a leveraged strategy.

questions.curriculum_ref: Framework for Evaluating YC Strategies — leveraged investor risk

questions.stem: A framework that combines the fixed-income expected-return decomposition with portfolio duration and convexity and with cross-currency return relationships most likely:

options.A: Excludes foreign-currency positions.
options.B: Quantifies level, slope, shape, and currency effects on portfolio value.

rationales.A: The cross-currency return relationships are what extend the framework to foreign-currency positions. The domestic-currency return is built from the foreign-currency return and the currency return, and multi-currency portfolio duration aggregates interest rate exposures across markets, so foreign bonds sit inside the framework rather than outside it.
rationales.B: The expected return of a fixed-income portfolio is summarized by the return decomposition, whose inputs under an active strategy rely on the manager's own expectations. Unexpected changes to the level, slope, and shape of the yield curve, and currency changes, can affect a portfolio's value in a number of ways, and the framework quantifies them through portfolio duration and convexity statistics for a single-currency portfolio and through the multi-currency extension for a portfolio holding foreign bonds.
rationales.C: Convexity enters alongside duration, so second-order price effects are part of the quantification. That is exactly why two portfolios with the same duration but different convexity, 40.229 against 26.5, do not respond identically even to a parallel shift, and why price change is not treated as linear in yield.

questions.curriculum_ref: Framework for Evaluating YC Strategies — integrated approach

questions.stem: A cross-currency carry trade is most likely:

options.A: Unhedged and most successful in stable, low-volatility markets.
options.B: Hedged and low-risk.

rationales.A: Carry trades are unhedged and are most successful in stable, low-volatility markets, because unforeseen market volatility can quickly erase even the most attractive cross-currency carry opportunity. In the first quarter of 2020, at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Mexican peso depreciated against the US dollar by approximately 25% in just over a month, a move far larger than any plausible interest differential earned over that period.
rationales.B: Hedging the currency exposure with a forward contract removes the source of the expected gain, since the forward is priced off the interest rate differential and gives back precisely what the trade is reaching for. The position is therefore left unhedged and carries the full currency risk, which is what makes it a carry trade rather than a low-risk one.
rationales.C: Profitability depends on the funding and investment currencies staying stable over the holding period. A sharp depreciation of the high-yield currency can produce a loss many times the interest differential earned, as the roughly 25% peso move in early 2020 demonstrated.

questions.curriculum_ref: Framework for Evaluating YC Strategies — carry trade risk

questions.stem: A manager running static yield curve strategies instead faces a yield curve inversion in which long-term yields decline and short-term yields rise sharply. The least likely outcome is:

options.A: A mark-to-market loss on shorter-maturity holdings.
options.B: A loss on the roll-down strategy.
options.C: A loss on the repo carry trade.

rationales.A: Sharply higher short-term yields push down the prices of the shorter-maturity positions held under the static strategies, so this loss is a likely consequence of the inversion rather than an unlikely one.
rationales.B: Rolling down the yield curve is a long-duration position in longer-maturity bonds, so a decline in long-term yields produces price appreciation, not a loss, making this the least likely outcome of the three. The other static strategies fare worse under the inversion. A repo carry trade breaks down because the short-term financing rate rises while the long-term yield earned falls, so the spread the trade depends on collapses or turns negative. Shorter-maturity cash positions take mark-to-market losses as short rates rise sharply. A buy-and-hold position at the long end is at least protected on a mark-to-market basis by the fall in long-term yields, but it does not benefit from the roll-down the manager was positioned for under static conditions.
rationales.C: An inversion lifts the repo financing rate while the long-term yield being earned falls, so the trade's funding cost rises against its income and the spread it relies on disappears. That loss is a likely outcome, so it is not the answer to a least likely question.

questions.stem: The combined risk and return impact of rolldown return versus carry, changes in the level, slope, and shape of a single-currency yield curve, and extension to multiple currencies is most likely best illustrated by:

options.A: A pair of integrated quantitative scenarios.
options.B: Purely qualitative discussion.

rationales.A: The fixed-income portfolio risk and return impact of rolldown return versus carry, changes in the level, slope, and shape of a single-currency yield curve, and the extension to multiple currencies, where spot and forward exchange rates are related to relative interest rates, is best illustrated with a pair of worked examples. The first takes two duration-matched single-currency Treasury portfolios through a bear steepening and a bull flattening, showing losses of 2.407% and 3.518% and gains of 2.473% and 3.891%. The second compares a bullet with a barbell in a foreign currency, combining rolldown, a parallel shift and a currency return into a domestic-currency total return. Between them the two exercise every term of the expected-return decomposition.
rationales.B: Qualitative discussion alone cannot show that two portfolios with identical duration of 4.88 lose 2.407% and 3.518% in the same steepening, nor how a 0.25% currency return compounds with a foreign-currency return. Quantified scenarios covering rolldown versus carry, curve level, slope and shape changes, and currency effects are what make those differences visible.
rationales.C: Duration captures only the first-order response to a parallel shift. It misses slope and shape effects, convexity, rolldown return and currency return, which is precisely the gap the integrated scenarios are constructed to fill.

questions.curriculum_ref: Framework for Evaluating YC Strategies — pair of examples

questions.stem: Active yield curve management most likely generates excess return by:

options.A: implementing curve views through cash bonds alone, avoiding derivatives.
options.B: positioning for parallel level shifts alone, ignoring slope and shape.
options.C: integrating level, slope, and shape views using cash and derivatives.

rationales.A: Futures, swaps, and options are central instruments in active curve management, not optional extras. A duration adjustment expressed with bond futures or a receive-fixed interest rate swap is cheaper, faster, and more capital efficient than the equivalent cash bond purchases and sales, and options are the only efficient way to express a view on yield volatility or on the value of embedded options. Avoiding derivatives to escape counterparty and margin complexity forfeits efficient implementation and leaves much of the toolkit unused, so it is not a characteristic of managers who successfully generate excess return.
rationales.B: Level, slope, and shape are distinct and separately tradable sources of return. A manager confined to parallel level shifts can adjust duration through bullets, barbells, or synthetic duration, but has no way to express a slope view through a steepener or flattener, no way to express a shape view through a butterfly, and no framework for detecting shaping risk between portfolio and benchmark through key rate durations. Even if level movements explain a large share of yield variance, slope and curvature views are integral to the strategy set, so treating them as an unnecessary complication leaves most of the toolkit unused.
rationales.C: Successful active yield curve management integrates the full set of views and tools: (1) a yield level view driving bullet, barbell, and synthetic duration adjustments; (2) a slope view driving steepener and flattener strategies; (3) a shape view driving butterfly strategies; (4) a volatility view driving the choice of options and of bonds with embedded options; (5) key rate duration analysis to detect shaping risk between the portfolio and its benchmark, which effective duration alone cannot reveal; (6) cross-currency strategies, where divergence from uncovered interest rate parity provides carry opportunities while exchange rate volatility can undermine profitability, with covered interest rate parity and cross-currency swaps used to hedge or to price the exposure; and (7) scenario analysis to quantify tail risk and stress-test positions against adverse outcomes. Convexity effects are accounted for where relevant, because two portfolios with the same duration can respond very differently to a large yield move. This holistic framework, rather than any single instrument or any single view, is what distinguishes managers who generate excess return.
